title: Laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair
subtitle: TEP and TAPP preperitoneal mesh repair

sources.title: International guidelines for groin hernia management
Guidelines for laparoscopic (TAPP) and endoscopic (TEP) treatment of inguinal hernia

sources.org: Daes J, Felix E (Annals of Surgery)
sources.title: Critical view of the myopectoral orifice

indications: Symptomatic inguinal hernia in a patient fit for general anaesthesia, where laparoscopic expertise is available.
Bilateral inguinal hernias, which can be repaired through the same access.
Recurrent hernia after a previous open anterior repair: a posterior approach works in an unscarred plane.
Women with groin hernia, because a femoral hernia is common and is covered by the same mesh.
TAPP may be used selectively for incarcerated hernias, where the contents can be inspected from inside.
contraindications: Unfit for general anaesthesia: an open repair under local anaesthesia is the alternative.
Previous extensive lower abdominal or pelvic surgery in the preperitoneal space (for example radical prostatectomy) is a relative contraindication and needs an experienced surgeon.
Strangulated hernia with suspected bowel necrosis or contamination: plan for an open approach or a TAPP inspection with a change of mesh plan.
Large irreducible scrotal hernias are relative contraindications and are better approached open by most surgeons.
preparation: Examine both groins standing and lying; a contralateral hernia changes the plan.
Ask the patient to pass urine immediately before theatre; catheterise only if the operation will be long or the bladder is full.
Review previous surgery and any lower abdominal scars before choosing TEP or TAPP.

Consent must include recurrence, chronic groin pain, seroma, haematoma including scrotal haematoma, urinary retention, injury to the vas and testicular vessels with testicular atrophy, bladder, bowel and major vessel injury, conversion to open, and port-site hernia.
Discuss mesh implantation and that the contralateral side may be repaired only if consented in advance.
positioning: Supine, both arms tucked at the sides so the surgeon and camera holder can stand on the opposite side to the hernia.
Slight Trendelenburg to move the bowel out of the pelvis, with the patient secured to the table.
Monitor at the foot of the table.
equipment: Laparoscopic stack, 10 mm 30 degree telescope, two 5 mm working ports and atraumatic graspers.
Balloon dissector for TEP if the unit uses one.
Flat mesh of adequate size (at least 10 by 15 cm), and the fixation device or glue the unit uses.
Sutures or tacks for TAPP peritoneal closure, and a Veress needle to vent a TEP pneumoperitoneum.
anatomy: The myopectoral orifice is bounded by the conjoint tendon above, the iliopsoas laterally, the rectus sheath medially and Cooper's ligament below; all groin hernias pass through it.

Indirect hernias lie lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels at the deep ring, direct hernias medial to them, femoral hernias below the iliopubic tract medial to the femoral vein, and obturator hernias in the obturator foramen.
The triangle of doom lies between the vas deferens and the gonadal vessels and contains the external iliac artery and vein.
The triangle of pain lies lateral to the gonadal vessels below the iliopubic tract and contains the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
The corona mortis is an anastomosis between the obturator and inferior epigastric or external iliac vessels, crossing Cooper's ligament, present in a significant minority of patients.
The space of Retzius lies behind the pubis in front of the bladder; the preperitoneal space continues laterally as the space of Bogros.
criticalSafety: Clear the whole myopectoral orifice so that all hernia sites, including femoral and obturator, are seen and covered.
Never use energy or fixation in the triangle of doom or the triangle of pain.
Parietalise the cord adequately so the lower mesh edge lies flat.
Close every peritoneal defect in TAPP so no mesh is exposed and no bowel is trapped.
Empty the bladder before starting medial dissection.
structuresAtRisk: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and genitofemoral nerve
Bowel, at access and in TAPP
commonErrors: Mesh too small, or not covering the femoral space.
Inadequate parietalisation, so the mesh rolls up on deflation.
Missed cord lipoma, mistaken later for recurrence.
Tacks placed below the iliopubic tract laterally, causing neuralgia.
Unclosed peritoneal gap in TAPP, causing small bowel obstruction.
complications: Seroma in the old sac space, usually resolving without aspiration.
Recurrence, most often due to an inadequate mesh or dissection.
Injury to the bladder, bowel, vas, testicular vessels or iliac vessels.
Port-site hernia and, after TAPP, small bowel obstruction from a peritoneal gap.
Mesh infection, uncommon after laparoscopic repair.
postop: Usually a day case; discharge when passing urine and comfortable.
Regular simple analgesia; return to normal activity as comfort allows, without a fixed lifting restriction for most patients.
Explain that a seroma in the groin or a scrotal bruise is common and usually settles.
Review new burning or shooting groin pain early; it may be nerve injury from fixation.
Seek review urgently for abdominal distension, vomiting or fever after TAPP.

steps.emphasis: Mark the side, examine both groins and confirm consent for the contralateral side if a second defect may be repaired.
Both arms tucked, slight Trendelenburg, bladder emptied immediately before theatre.
TAPP: open umbilical access. TEP: go to the next step instead, and use the Veress only to vent an accidental pneumoperitoneum.
In TAPP, inspect both myopectoral orifices from inside before raising any flap, and the contents of any incarcerated hernia.
Convert to TAPP or open if the TEP space keeps collapsing or the landmarks cannot be defined; convert to open for uncontrolled bleeding.
Indirect sacs are reduced off the cord; direct sacs and the pseudosac of transversalis fascia are reduced from the defect. Look for and reduce a cord lipoma.
Close the anterior rectus sheath at the TEP camera site and every port of 10 mm or more.

step.lih.tep-space.title: TEP: entering and developing the preperitoneal space
step.lih.tep-space.why: In TEP the whole operation happens in a space that does not exist until you make it. Entering the correct plane behind the rectus muscle, in front of the posterior sheath, keeps the peritoneum intact and the bowel out of the field.
how: Make a small infraumbilical incision, incise the anterior rectus sheath on the side of the hernia and retract the rectus muscle laterally.
Pass a balloon dissector or the telescope along the anterior surface of the posterior rectus sheath towards the pubis, in the midline behind the muscle.
Inflate under vision and watch the inferior epigastric vessels stay up on the muscle; stop if they are being stripped down.
Insufflate the space at the low pressure your unit uses, and place the two working ports in the midline under vision, below the camera port.
If the peritoneum tears and the space collapses, vent the pneumoperitoneum with a Veress needle at the umbilicus, close the tear with a loop or clip, or convert to TAPP.
structuresAtRisk: Peritoneum, tear causing loss of working space
Bladder, during midline dissection towards the pubis
pitfalls: Entering the peritoneum at the posterior sheath and then working with a collapsing space.
Stripping the inferior epigastric vessels off the rectus muscle with the balloon.
Placing the lowest midline port so low that it enters the bladder.

step.lih.peritoneal-flap.title: TAPP: raising the peritoneal flap
step.lih.peritoneal-flap.why: The flap opens the preperitoneal space from inside and must later cover the mesh completely. A flap placed too low, or torn, leaves mesh exposed to bowel.
how: Incise the peritoneum from the medial umbilical ligament to the anterior superior iliac spine, a few centimetres above the defect and the deep ring.
Develop the upper flap down in the areolar plane anterior to the transversalis fascia, then the lower flap, keeping the peritoneum intact.
Preserve the medial umbilical ligament unless it obstructs the view, and stay above the iliopubic tract laterally while raising the flap.
Keep the peritoneum as an intact sheet; a hole now becomes a gap over the mesh later.
structuresAtRisk: Inferior epigastric vessels in the upper flap
pitfalls: Starting the incision too low, over the defect, which leaves no flap to close.
Tearing the flap while hurrying, then struggling to close it over the mesh.

step.lih.landmarks.title: Defining the myopectoral orifice and its danger zones
step.lih.landmarks.why: From behind, the groin is a different anatomy. Clearing the whole myopectoral orifice exposes every potential hernia site, and naming the triangle of doom and the triangle of pain before stapling or tacking prevents the major vascular and chronic pain injuries.
how: Clear the space of Retzius medially to the pubic symphysis and Cooper's ligament, crossing the midline in a bilateral repair.
Identify the inferior epigastric vessels, the iliopubic tract, the vas deferens (or round ligament) and the gonadal vessels.

Name the triangle of doom between the vas and the gonadal vessels, containing the external iliac vessels, and the triangle of pain lateral to the gonadal vessels below the iliopubic tract, containing the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
Look for and record direct, indirect, femoral and obturator defects on both sides before reducing anything.
Watch for the corona mortis, an anastomotic vessel crossing Cooper's ligament, before dissecting or fixing on the ligament.
structuresAtRisk: Bladder in the space of Retzius
pitfalls: Dissecting in the triangle of doom with an energy device.
Stripping the fascia overlying the nerves in the triangle of pain.
Missing a femoral or obturator defect because the medial space was not cleared.

step.lih.parietalisation.title: Parietalisation of the cord structures
step.lih.parietalisation.why: The lower edge of the mesh can only lie flat if the peritoneum is lifted well off the vas and gonadal vessels. Inadequate parietalisation is a leading technical cause of recurrence after laparoscopic repair, because the peritoneum rolls the mesh up as the space deflates.
how: After reducing the indirect sac, continue separating the peritoneum from the vas and the gonadal vessels proximally, well beyond the deep ring.
Dissect with blunt instruments along the cord structures; avoid diathermy on the vas and the vessels.
Continue until the peritoneal edge lies clear of the area the lower mesh edge will cover, so the mesh lies on the psoas and iliac vessels without being lifted.
If a large indirect sac cannot be fully reduced, divide it beyond the deep ring and close the proximal peritoneum, leaving the distal part open.
structuresAtRisk: External iliac vessels deep to the cord
pitfalls: Stopping parietalisation at the deep ring, so the mesh edge rolls up.
Grasping the vas directly with a toothed instrument.
Ignoring a cord lipoma, which presents as a lump at review.

step.lih.mesh-place.title: Positioning and fixing the mesh in the preperitoneal space
step.lih.mesh-place.why: The mesh must cover the whole myopectoral orifice, direct, indirect and femoral spaces, with overlap. Fixation, where used, is placed only in safe zones: a tack in the triangle of doom bleeds and a tack in the triangle of pain causes chronic neuralgia.
how: Introduce a mesh of adequate size; HerniaSurge recommends at least 10 by 15 cm for an adult.
Position it to overlap the pubic symphysis medially, cover Cooper's ligament and the femoral canal, and lie lateral to the deep ring, with the lower edge lying on the parietalised peritoneum.
Decide on fixation by hernia type: it can often be omitted in TEP and TAPP, and is generally advised for large direct defects. Follow the guideline your unit uses.

If fixing, place tacks or glue only into Cooper's ligament and the anterior abdominal wall above the iliopubic tract; never below the iliopubic tract lateral to the vessels, and never in the triangles of doom or pain.
Palpate the abdominal wall from outside when tacking to feel the tip, and avoid going deep near the inferior epigastric vessels.
structuresAtRisk: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve
pitfalls: A mesh too small to cover the femoral space.
Tacking below the iliopubic tract laterally.
A mesh slit around the cord in a laparoscopic repair, which creates a recurrence site; a flat mesh with full parietalisation is the norm.

step.lih.flap-closure.title: Closing the peritoneum and deflating under vision
step.lih.flap-closure.why: Exposed mesh adheres to bowel, and a gap in the peritoneal closure can trap a loop of bowel. In TEP, the mesh can curl as the space deflates unless its lower edge is watched.
how: TAPP: close the peritoneal flap completely over the mesh with a running suture or tacks, leaving no gap and no mesh exposed.
Close any tear in the peritoneum found during the dissection.
Desufflate the preperitoneal space under vision while holding the lower edge of the mesh down with an instrument, so it is not rolled up by the peritoneum.
Before closing, inspect the space of Retzius, the epigastric vessels and the cord at low pressure for bleeding.
Confirm both sides are covered in a bilateral repair before the camera is removed.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel trapped in a peritoneal gap
pitfalls: A partial flap closure with mesh visible at one corner.
Removing the instruments before watching the mesh during desufflation.
